title: Cask strength whisky explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What cask strength whisky means, why its ABV varies from bottle to bottle and how to taste it with water without numbing your palate.
teaser: Cask strength whisky is bottled the way it left the cask. That makes it bolder and a little more demanding.
standfirst: Most whisky is diluted to around 40% ABV before bottling. Cask strength whisky is not. It reaches the bottle at whatever strength it had in the cask, often well over 50%. Here is what that means and how to enjoy it sensibly.
sections:
Cask strength, sometimes called barrel proof in the United States, means the whisky was bottled without being reduced with water after maturation. It may still be filtered to remove char and wood particles. What it does not get is the dilution that brings most whiskies down to 40 to 46% ABV.

The result is usually somewhere between about 50 and 65% ABV, depending on the filling strength, the length of maturation and the warehouse. Our guide to whisky label terms covers the other words on the bottle.

Spirit is usually filled into casks at a set strength. Many Scotch distilleries choose around 63.5% ABV. From there, maturation changes it. In cool, humid warehouses, alcohol evaporates faster than water and strength falls slowly over the years. In hot, dry warehouses, water can evaporate faster and strength may hold or even rise.

So two casks of the same spirit, filled on the same day, can come out at different strengths. A cask strength release reports whatever the casks gave. Batch to batch, the number on the label moves. Our guide to humidity and strength change explains the science.

• Control. You decide how much water to add, rather than the distiller.
  • Intensity. More alcohol carries more aroma compounds, so flavours can feel bigger.
  • Fewer bottling steps. Cask strength whiskies are often not chill filtered, keeping compounds some drinkers value for texture.
  • A glimpse of the cask. It is the closest most drinkers get to tasting from the warehouse.

None of this makes it better whisky by default. It makes it a different experience. It rewards a bit of care.

Cask strength also says nothing about age. A young whisky filled at high strength into an active cask can be bottled at cask strength after a few years. An old whisky from a damp warehouse may have drifted down to the high 40s. Check the age statement separately.

At 55 to 60% ABV, alcohol can overwhelm your nose and numb your tongue. Sniff too hard and you will get a burning sensation rather than aromas. Sip a full mouthful neat and the next three whiskies will taste of nothing.

The answer is technique, not bravery. Nose gently with the glass held slightly below your nose. Take a very small first sip and let it coat the mouth before swallowing. Then add water. Our guide to tasting cask strength whisky goes through it step by step.

Start with a few drops from a pipette or straw, stir and nose again. Keep going a little at a time. Many tasters find a whisky opens up somewhere between 40 and 46% ABV, but there is no correct point. Some whiskies change dramatically with water. Others barely move.

A rough guide: a 30 millilitre measure at 60% ABV, plus 10 millilitres of water, comes to 45% ABV. Plus 15 millilitres, it is 40%. Use clean, still water at room temperature. Very hard or chlorinated tap water can dull aromas.

Packaged still water or water from a home RO filter works well. Keep a small jug for the tasting, with a pipette or a teaspoon, so each addition is small and repeatable.

A measure of cask strength whisky carries noticeably more alcohol than the same measure at 40%. A 30 millilitre pour at 60% ABV holds 18 millilitres of pure alcohol, against 12 millilitres at 40%. Pour smaller measures, keep a glass of water alongside, pace yourself and never drink and drive. Adding water to the whisky does not reduce the alcohol you drink. It just spreads it out.

Indian warehouses run hot. Depending on the site, Indian-matured cask strength whiskies may show strength that has held up or risen, along with plenty of wood from fast extraction. That makes water even more useful. Many Indian drinkers already add water or ice to whisky, which suits cask strength well, though ice also numbs aroma. Try water first, ice second. Our guide to how whisky is made covers the steps that lead to the cask.

Pour three small measures of the same cask strength whisky. Leave one neat, add a few drops of water to the second and a teaspoon to the third. Nose them in order and write down one aroma that appears or disappears at each step. That single exercise will teach you how your palate responds to strength better than any rule of thumb.
faqs: Whisky bottled without being diluted with water after maturation, usually at 50 to 65% ABV.
Why does cask strength whisky vary in ABV?
Each cask's strength changes during maturation depending on warehouse humidity and temperature, so batches come out at different strengths.
Should I add water to cask strength whisky?
Usually yes, a little at a time. Water opens aromas and protects your palate, though it does not reduce the alcohol you drink.
